name: Cucuteni–Trypillia culture
title: The story of the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture

text: About 7,000 years ago, a farming people began to spread out from the land around the Prut river.
They settled from the Carpathian Mountains to the Dnieper river, in today’s Moldova, Ukraine and Romania.
src: c. 5050 BCE: The Cucuteni–Trypillia culture takes shape from earlier farming cultures in the region between the Prut and the Siret
From the Carpathian Mountains to the Dniester and Dnieper, about 350,000 km², centred on present-day Moldova with large parts of western Ukraine and north-eastern Romania

text: They grew wheat, barley, rye, millet, peas and beans, and kept cattle, pigs, sheep and goats.
src: growing club wheat, oats, rye, proso millet, barley, peas and beans, and kept mostly cattle, with fewer pigs, sheep and goats

text: Some of their villages grew huge, with up to three thousand buildings, among the biggest in Europe and Asia.
Every 60 to 80 years people burned their villages and built them again, and nobody knows for sure why.
src: some grew into “mega-sites” with as many as three thousand structures / the largest settlements in Eurasia at the time
Its settlements were burned and rebuilt every 60 to 80 years, sometimes on the plan of the old buildings, for reasons scholars still debate

text: Potters painted swirling spirals in black, red and yellow, and people made tools of stone, bone and later copper.
They also made little clay animals and cups on four wheels, which may have been toys.
src: Middle-period vessels carry spirals painted in black on yellow and red / Tools were of flint, stone, bone, antler and horn and, later, copper
miniature animals and cups on four wheels, often thought to be toys

text: Late in their history, herders from the steppe, the grasslands to the east, came to live beside them.
Their way of life ended almost 5,000 years ago, and experts still argue about why.
src: Ancient DNA shows steppe-related ancestry entering the population in its late phase, perhaps as early as 3500 BCE, through long contact and gradual mixing / Yamnaya settlements living for a time beside Cucuteni–Trypillia ones in the east / the people of the Kurgan culture, the Yamnaya and their forerunners of the Pontic–Caspian steppe / as large populations turned woodland toward grassland
c. 2950 BCE: The Cucuteni–Trypillia culture comes to an end, in circumstances still debated

text: Archaeologists, people who dig up the past, have found about 3,000 of their sites.
Their painted pots and clay figures are kept in museums in Ukraine, Romania and Russia.
src: The largest collections are in museums in Russia, Ukraine and Romania / Pottery is the culture’s best-known work / Clay figurines of women and animals
